analysis.one_liner: Creates universal government-guaranteed health coverage for every resident, financed by higher income, corporate, payroll, and alcohol and tobacco taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced in October 1991 by Rep. Harry Johnston with 6 Democratic cosponsors, it sat in two House committees and was sent to a health subcommittee, where it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a national health insurance program giving every U.S. citizen and permanent resident guaranteed coverage through state-administered plans, run locally by elected-style health care district boards. It would cover hospital care, doctor visits, prescription drugs, preventive screenings, mental health care, and long-term care, with no deductibles and caps on out-of-pocket costs, and it would replace Medicare, Medicaid, federal employee coverage, military coverage, and veterans' health benefits. To pay for it, the bill would raise individual income tax rates, raise the top corporate tax rate from 34% to 44%, raise the Medicare payroll tax while trimming the Social Security portion, and sharply increase excise taxes on cigarettes and liquor.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. citizen and permanent resident would gain guaranteed comprehensive health coverage with no deductibles, coinsurance capped at $1,000 per person per year (with allowances for low-income families), free preventive and maternity services, and a new entitlement to long-term care including nursing home, home health, and respite care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents, especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Every citizen and permanent resident would be entitled to enroll in a state health plan covering hospital care, physician services, prescription drugs, diagnostics, family planning, hospice, dialysis, prosthetics, and more [S2][S3].
The bill prohibits deductibles entirely and caps annual coinsurance at $1,000 per individual or $1,500 per family, with adjustments for families earning under 200% of the poverty line [S3].

It creates a new entitlement to long-term care — nursing home care, home and community-based services, and up to 720 hours a year of in-home respite care for family caregivers — covering needs Medicare largely leaves to families [S2][S3].
Preventive services including mammograms, Pap smears, colorectal screening, well-child care, and prenatal care would be covered without coinsurance [S3].
Providers would have to accept the plan's payment as payment in full, ending balance billing against patients [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers broadly: individual income tax rates would rise (a 30% bracket starting near $32,000 for joint filers and a 34% top rate), the top corporate rate would go from 34% to 44%, the Medicare payroll tax would rise to 1.95% on wages up to a higher $125,000 base, and cigarette taxes would more than double while liquor taxes nearly quadrupled [S3].

drawbacks.text: The financing is a broad tax increase that reaches middle-income households, not only the wealthy: a 30% marginal rate would begin at roughly $32,450 for a married couple filing jointly, and every bracket would start with a 16% rate [S3].

State plans would be subject to hard annual budget limits — total payments could not exceed the state plan budget, except for emergency services — which could force rationing of care or lower provider payments when demand exceeded the budget [S3].

The bill would terminate Medicare, Medicaid, federal employee health benefits, CHAMPUS, and veterans' health benefits and fold them into the new system, a large transition with real risk of disruption for people currently covered [S3].

As a condition of federal payment, states would have to shift malpractice liability from individual doctors to hospitals and bar punitive damages entirely, which supporters called cost control and critics saw as weakened accountability for negligent care [S3].

States that did not set up their own plan would receive only half the federal payment while the federal board ran their plan, giving states a strong financial push to accept a system many might resist [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is substantial: universal coverage with no deductibles, hard caps on out-of-pocket costs, and a long-term care benefit that does not exist anywhere in the current system. The cost is honestly large — the bill raises income, corporate, payroll, and excise taxes across the board, and its hard annual budget caps plus mandatory assignment (doctors must accept the plan rate as payment in full) meant the gains in access would come with real risk of constrained supply and squeezed provider payments. It was also an unusually sweeping restructuring that would terminate five existing federal health programs at once, which is a legitimate transition concern even for supporters of universal coverage.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, sent to a health subcommittee two and a half weeks later, and never received a markup, hearing, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Harry Johnston of Florida introduced the bill on October 31, 1991, for himself and Rep. Barbara Boxer [S1][S3][S5].
It was referred jointly to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced [S1][S5].
On November 18, 1991, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment — the last action of any kind recorded for the bill [S5].
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a markup, a hearing vote, or a floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing health insurance arrangement continued unchanged — private insurers kept their role, employers kept their coverage obligations, and no new broad taxes were enacted. Members of Congress never had to cast a recorded vote on universal coverage or on the tax increases that would fund it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing insurance system and its payers

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats ever put their names on the bill (a sponsor plus 6 Democratic cosponsors), and because it never reached the floor, no vote ever recorded where the parties stood.

industries.note: The default design makes the local district board the single community insurer, the exclusive payer for covered services; private plans could continue only under strict agreements, paid fixed per-capita amounts by the district, with open enrollment and no health-based discrimination. This is a cheaper public alternative that would displace much of the private insurance market.

Universal enrollment would end uncompensated care and guarantee payment, but district boards would negotiate rates with each institution and enforce hard annual budget caps, while Medicare and Medicaid payment streams would be replaced.

Every resident would become a covered patient, but fee schedules would be set through negotiation with practitioner organizations, doctors would have to accept the plan rate as payment in full, and malpractice liability would shift to hospitals with punitive damages barred — a trade of payment predictability for controlled fees.

industries.industry: Tobacco manufacturers and distilled spirits producers
industries.note: Cigarette excise taxes would more than double and the liquor tax would rise from $13.50 to $50 per proof gallon, with retroactive floor-stock taxes on inventory; these costs would be passed to consumers but the industries bear the tax directly.

The top corporate rate would rise from 34% to 44% and the top individual rate to 34%, though employers would also shed most of their role funding private health coverage and would see the Social Security payroll share cut to 5.7%.
